notes.meaning: David confronts Doeg the Edomite, calling him a 'mighty man' with biting sarcasm for killing defenseless priests. A wicked person may brag about causing harm, but that pride is completely empty because God's faithful love never stops guarding His people. Earthly tyrants come and go, but God's goodness outlasts them all.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that true strength is meant for doing good rather than causing harm, noting that even a small scorpion can kill, so believers should boast only in the Lord.

notes.meaning: Cruel and lying words reveal an evil heart. David compares the deceitful tongue to a razor that seems to shave smoothly but secretly cuts deep to murder. Doeg pretended to be a loyal servant reporting facts, but he was really using slander to send innocent people to their deaths.

The wicked person deliberately turns away from goodness and falls in love with falsehood and destruction. Their words act like a hungry beast, swallowing up the lives, reputations, and homes of the innocent. Choosing deceit over truth twists a person's character until they actively delight in ruining others.

God promises a complete and sudden end to the proud oppressor. He will tear down the wrongdoer like a broken building, sweep him away like a burning coal, and pull him up by the roots like a dead tree. The destroyer who wiped out others will be utterly removed from his home and from life on earth.

God's people will watch the tyrant fall and feel deep, holy awe toward God's righteous judgment. They will also laugh at his ruin, not out of petty spite, but with joyful relief that God has brought justice and exposed evil as total foolishness. Seeing the wicked collapse strengthens the faith of believers and reminds them to revere the Lord.

The godly point to the fallen oppressor as an object lesson for everyone else. He refused to look to God for safety, choosing instead to trust in his stolen riches and strengthen himself through violent schemes. In the end, wealth and cruelty cannot protect anyone who refuses God as their shelter.

While the wicked are uprooted and thrown away, David compares himself to a fresh olive tree thriving in God's presence. Olive trees live long, fruitful lives in good soil, picturing the lasting spiritual strength of someone who stays near the Lord. Instead of trusting in fleeting riches, the believer safely rests in God's steadfast love forever.

David promises to give God unending praise because the Lord has already stepped in to save him and judge evil. He commits to patiently wait on God's name—meaning His faithful character and power—among the gathered community of believers. Resting quietly in God's promises brings peace to a troubled soul while waiting for full deliverance.
